title: Four ways to describe motion
prior_knowledge_summary: Students can measure length and time in SI units.
Students can describe everyday movement using position, direction and duration.
new_learning: Distance and displacement answer different questions about one journey.
Speed is scalar while velocity includes direction.
learning_outcomes: Define displacement and velocity using the accepted physics wording.
Distinguish distance from displacement in words, paths, diagrams and calculations.
Distinguish speed from velocity and include direction when it is needed.
Calculate average speed using total distance and total time.
Calculate average velocity using resultant displacement and total time.
Use signs or vector geometry to find displacement in one and two dimensions.
Apply these ideas inside unfamiliar, multi-stage motion stories.
scope_note: This lesson does not teach acceleration, motion graphs or constant-acceleration equations. Later exam questions may combine those ideas with speed and velocity, but they belong to later lessons.

definitions.text: distance in a specified direction from a point

formulas.name: Average speed
formulas.display: v_avg = total distance travelled / total time taken

canonical_demands_checked: Exact definitions of velocity and displacement.
Average speed from total path and average velocity from resultant displacement.
Drawing distinct distance-path and displacement-vector representations.
evidence_basis.originality_note: Lesson contexts and values are original. Canonical questions and diagrams supply the assessment forms and misconceptions.
evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked canonical question text, mark schemes and relevant path/vector diagram. All mapped parts are relevant.

blocks.title: The whistle blows
body: It is sports day. Zain starts at the line of a 400 m running track. He runs one complete lap and crosses the same line again.
The coach says, 'You travelled 400 m.' His physics teacher says, 'Your displacement is zero.'
Zain is confused. He ran hard for a full lap. How can anything about his motion be zero?
Keep this puzzle in mind. We will solve it by describing motion in four different ways.

figure.purpose: Create the conflict between a long journey and an unchanged final position.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn top view of a simple oval 400 m track. Zain starts and finishes at the same marked line. One arrow follows a complete lap. Labels: start, finish and 400 m path.
figure.alt_text: Zain completes one 400 metre lap and returns to the starting line.

blocks.title: 1. Distance measures the whole path
body: Imagine tracing Zain's route with a marker. The line goes all the way around the track. The length of that line is the distance travelled.
For one lap, distance = 400 m. Every metre counts. Turning around the track does not remove any distance.
Distance answers: How much ground did the object cover?
Distance has magnitude but no direction. It is a scalar.
blocks.remember: Distance follows the whole path. It is a scalar.

blocks.title: 2. Displacement compares two positions
blocks.definition: distance in a specified direction from a point
body: Ignore the shape of the track. Look only at Zain's starting point and finishing point. He finishes exactly where he started.
The chosen point is called a reference point. After one complete lap, Zain is 0 m from the start line, so displacement = 0 m.
This does not mean Zain did not move. It means his final position is the same as his initial position.
Displacement answers: Where is the finish compared with the start? A non-zero displacement needs magnitude and direction, so it is a vector.
blocks.remember: Displacement compares the final position with the reference point. It is a vector, so direction matters.

figure.purpose: Compare distance and displacement for one complete lap.
figure.brief: Two side-by-side sketches of the oval track. Left: complete path highlighted and labelled distance = 400 m. Right: shared start and finish point labelled displacement = 0 m.
figure.alt_text: A full lap has a distance of 400 metres and zero displacement.

blocks.title: A straight sprint
body: Zain runs 100 m east in a straight line and does not turn back.
distance = 100 m
displacement = 100 m east
The magnitudes are equal because he moves in one straight direction. Displacement still needs direction.

figure.purpose: Show the special case where distance and displacement have equal magnitudes.
figure.brief: Straight 100 m lane from start to finish, pointing east. Show the route line and direct vector over the same line. Label distance = 100 m and displacement = 100 m east.
figure.alt_text: A straight 100 metre sprint east with equal distance and displacement magnitudes.

blocks.title: A turn changes the answer
body: Zain walks 30 m east to collect his bag, then walks 10 m west for his water bottle.
distance = 30 + 10 = 40 m
displacement = 20 m east
Distance remembers every part of the route. Displacement remembers only the overall change in position.

figure.purpose: Separate path addition from overall position change.
figure.brief: Horizontal number line. Start at 0 m, bag at 30 m east, final point at 20 m east. Show 30 m east and 10 m west path arrows plus a direct 20 m east displacement arrow.
figure.alt_text: A 30 metre east and 10 metre west journey has distance 40 metres and displacement 20 metres east.

blocks.title: Using signs for direction
body: On a straight line, signs can represent opposite directions. Let east be positive, so west is negative.
displacement = (+30) + (-10) = +20 m
The positive sign means east because east was chosen as positive. We could choose west as positive instead. The signs would change, but the physical result would not.
Always identify the positive direction and use it consistently.

blocks.title: 3. Speed tells us how quickly distance changes
blocks.formula: v_avg = total distance travelled / total time taken
blocks.units: Distance in m, time in s, average speed in m s^-1.
body: Zain and Omar each run one 400 m lap. Zain takes 80 s and Omar takes 100 s.
Zain: average speed = 400 / 80 = 5.0 m s^-1
Omar: average speed = 400 / 100 = 4.0 m s^-1
Speed has magnitude but no direction. It is a scalar.
blocks.remember: Average speed uses total distance and total time. It does not use displacement.

figure.purpose: Show that covering the same distance in less time gives greater average speed.
figure.brief: Zain and Omar on matching 400 m tracks. Label Zain 80 s and 5.0 m s^-1. Label Omar 100 s and 4.0 m s^-1.
figure.alt_text: Two runners cover the same distance in different times and have different average speeds.

blocks.title: Why do we say average speed?
body: Zain did not move at exactly 5.0 m s^-1 at every moment. He accelerated at the start, changed speed around bends and slowed after the finish.
The value 5.0 m s^-1 describes the whole lap with one number. It is the constant speed that would cover the same total distance in the same total time.

blocks.title: Waiting time counts
body: Zain walks 120 m in 80 s, stops for 20 s, then walks 180 m in 100 s.
total distance = 120 + 180 = 300 m
total time = 80 + 20 + 100 = 200 s
average speed = 300 / 200 = 1.5 m s^-1
The stop is part of the journey, so its time is included.

blocks.title: 4. Velocity also tells us direction
body: Two runners pass the centre of the field at 6.0 m s^-1 in opposite directions. Their speeds are equal, but their motions are different.
Velocity tells us how quickly displacement changes. Since displacement includes direction, velocity includes direction too.
Speed asks: How fast? Velocity asks: How fast, and in which direction?
blocks.remember: Velocity describes how quickly displacement changes. A numerical velocity needs a direction unless a sign convention already shows it.

figure.purpose: Show why equal speeds do not describe opposite motion fully.
figure.brief: Two runners cross a field in opposite directions. Both speeds are 6.0 m s^-1. Add velocity arrows labelled 6.0 m s^-1 east and 6.0 m s^-1 west.
figure.alt_text: Two runners have equal speeds but opposite velocities.

blocks.title: Average velocity
blocks.units: Average velocity is measured in m s^-1 and needs a direction.
body: For Zain's 400 m lap, displacement = 0 m and time = 80 s.
average velocity = 0 / 80 = 0 m s^-1
He was moving. His average velocity is zero because his final position is his initial position.
Average speed uses total distance. Average velocity uses resultant displacement.
blocks.remember: A return to the starting point gives zero average velocity, not necessarily zero average speed.

figure.purpose: Connect average speed to distance and average velocity to displacement.
figure.brief: Same oval track. Show distance = 400 m and average speed = 5.0 m s^-1 beside the path. Show displacement = 0 m and average velocity = 0 m s^-1 beside the shared start and finish.
figure.alt_text: One full lap has non-zero average speed and zero average velocity.

blocks.title: One journey, both calculations
body: Zain runs 150 m east, then 50 m west, in 40 s.
distance = 150 + 50 = 200 m
average speed = 200 / 40 = 5.0 m s^-1
displacement = (+150) + (-50) = 100 m east
average velocity = 100 / 40 = 2.5 m s^-1 east
Distance counts outward and return movement. Displacement compares only the start and finish.

blocks.title: Do not simply average two speeds
body: If Zain runs one part at 3.0 m s^-1 and another at 7.0 m s^-1, the average speed is not automatically 5.0 m s^-1.
The result depends on the distance and time for each part. Always use total distance divided by total time.
A simple mean works only in special cases, such as equal time spent at each speed.

blocks.title: Motion in two directions
body: Zain walks 60 m east and then 80 m north.
distance = 60 + 80 = 140 m
magnitude of displacement = sqrt(60^2 + 80^2) = 100 m
angle north of east = tan^-1(80 / 60) = 53 degrees
displacement = 100 m at 53 degrees north of east

figure.purpose: Show path distance and direct vector displacement in two dimensions.
figure.brief: Right-angled route of 60 m east then 80 m north. Draw the direct diagonal vector, label it 100 m and mark 53 degrees north of east.
figure.alt_text: A right-angled journey has a 140 metre path and a 100 metre displacement.

blocks.title: The four-question method
items: Do I need the whole path? Use distance.
Do I need the overall change from start to finish? Use displacement.
Do I need total distance per total time? Use average speed.
Do I need resultant displacement per total time? Use average velocity and include direction.

blocks.title: Final idea
body: Zain's lap needs four descriptions.
The 400 m distance describes the path. The 0 m displacement describes the unchanged final position.
The 5.0 m s^-1 average speed describes how quickly he covered the path. The 0 m s^-1 average velocity describes his overall change in position per second.
One journey can have all four answers. The correct answer depends on the question physics is asking.

requirements: Do not add decorative crowds, buildings, trophies or scenery.

concepts_taught: Distance is the total length of the path travelled.
Displacement compares the initial and final positions and includes direction.
Speed is a scalar and velocity is a vector.
Average speed uses total distance and total time.
Average velocity uses resultant displacement and total time.
A chosen positive direction allows one-dimensional displacement and velocity to be represented with signs.
representations_used: average speed and average velocity calculations
misconceptions_addressed: Distance and displacement are always equal.
Returning to the start means no distance was travelled.
Average speed can always be found by taking the arithmetic mean of stage speeds.
Waiting time can be omitted from a whole-journey average.
skills_students_can_now_use: Use a sign convention to represent direction in one dimension.
Calculate average speed from total distance and total time.
Calculate average velocity from resultant displacement and total time.
Determine resultant displacement for simple one-dimensional and right-angled journeys.
next_lesson_can_assume: Positive and negative signs can represent opposite directions.
A change of direction is a change of velocity even if speed is unchanged.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: How acceleration direction relates to speeding up or slowing down.
